694.title: Where it didn't
694.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism look honestly at where it hasn't helped, and pair it with other support, such as friends, counseling, rest or a faith community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where it worked, as the Discourses promised it would. Your line was it worked here. Did you write down the moment you found, with the day or the place? Keep it close. Today we turn it over. Day six hundred ninety-four.

Nobody makes a poster of this part. Three in the morning, a year into the practice, someone lies awake who knows all the lines by now. Some things are up to us, some aren't. It isn't the thing, it's the judgment about the thing. They could recite them in their sleep, if they could sleep. And none of it is loosening the knot in the chest. The words sit there like a poster on a waiting-room wall. Yesterday we named where the porch helped. Today, just as plainly: where it didn't.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `ALL THE LINES, NO SLEEP.` → `WHERE IT DIDN'T HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the Stoics saw this coming. In the Discourses, Epictetus challenges his students: show me a Stoic, if you can. Not someone who can talk Stoic, but someone who is sick and happy, in danger and happy, disgraced and happy. He says he'd gladly see one, and implies he hasn't. And Marcus, writing to himself, expects to be knocked out of tune. When circumstances force you to be disturbed, he says, come back to yourself quickly, and don't stay out of tune longer than you must. We met that line on day five hundred seventy-five. The teachers didn't claim the method always worked, even on them. Second, where it can misfire. When it turns into small-s stoic: teeth gritted, feelings pushed down until they come out sideways. When up to us and not up to us becomes an excuse to shrug at something you could change, or something unfair that someone should challenge. And when the trouble is depression, a deep loss, or a body that needs care. A maxim is not a doctor, a friend, or a night's sleep. Third, two honest reasons. Sometimes the tool was fine and you were hungry, exhausted, or alone. Sometimes the tool was the wrong one for the job. Both are worth knowing, and neither is a failure of character. Fourth, why say it out loud. A practice that only reports its wins turns into a sales pitch. One that can say here, it didn't help stays a practice, something you use with open eyes.

segments.voice: Let one moment come where the porch didn't help. Choose one you can look at today; you don't have to open the heaviest one. Where were you? What did you reach for, and what happened? Then ask, gently: was I tired, hungry, alone? Or was this the wrong tool? Don't judge the answer. Just name it. If what comes up is heavy and still with you, that's a reason to talk to someone you trust, not to try harder alone. The bell holds the time.
Small-s stoic, when the practice curdles into teeth gritted and feelings pushed down until they come out sideways. Today's word.

Your line: honest about it. Next to yesterday's moment, write today's, in one sentence. Then add one thing that might help next time, whether it's sleep, a person, or a different tool. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: Ahead: the great questions
695.hook: year three turns to suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, across many traditions
695.howItsDone: Some people on their own spiritual path return again and again to a few great questions, reading what different traditions, philosophers and scientists say about each.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where it didn't, the small-s stoic kind. Your line was honest about it. Did you write the moment down, next to the one where it worked, with one thing that might help next time? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Some questions come up at four in the afternoon, between emails. Most don't. The big ones come in hospital corridors, at gravesides, on the night a baby is born, in the car after you've been let go, on a mountain when the clouds suddenly open. Why is there so much suffering? What happens when we die? Can I forgive this? Traditions all over the world have sat up late with those questions. Tomorrow the porch closes for the year. Today we look ahead.
screen: `HOSPITAL CORRIDORS, MOUNTAINTOPS.` → `THE QUESTIONS THAT COME AT NIGHT.` → `TODAY, WE LOOK AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the six. Year three is built around six questions: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, and awe. Not a new school this time, and not a single book. Six themes, each given room, one after another. Second, how it works. For each question, we'll hear many voices: scripture and saints, sages and poets, philosophers and scientists. Every voice is named. A line from the Psalms is the Psalms; a teaching of the Buddha is the Buddha's; a finding from a lab is the lab's. Nobody is blended into anybody else, and nobody is ranked. Where traditions see a question differently, and on death they really do, we say who says what, in their own words, and leave it there. Third, the porch comes too. The Stoics don't disappear. On death we've already sat with Marcus and the ripe olive that falls blessing the tree; on awe, with Marcus again, looking down from above. In year three they take a seat at a much bigger table, one voice among many. Fourth, questions to live with. In 1903 the poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young man who had asked him for advice. Be patient, he told him, with what is still unsettled in you. Love the questions themselves. Don't chase answers you aren't ready to live yet. Live the questions now, and one day you may find, almost without noticing, that you've grown into an answer. That's the spirit of year three. Not a quiz with answers in the back. A year of keeping good company with the hard questions.
screen: `SIX QUESTIONS, ONE AT A TIME.` · `MANY VOICES, EACH ONE NAMED.` · `THE STOICS AT A BIGGER TABLE.` · `LOVE THE QUESTIONS THEMSELVES.` · then, large: `THE BIG QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Let the six questions pass through you, one breath each. Suffering. Death. Love. Work. Forgiveness. Awe. Don't think hard about any of them. Just notice which one tugs, which one your body leans toward, or flinches from. That may be the one. When you've found it, let it stay. You don't need an answer. Just let the question sit beside you, like a companion for the road. The bell holds the time.
Ahead: year three, six great questions, suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, heard through many named voices. Today's word.
Your line: the big questions. Write the one you picked at the top of a fresh page, and leave the rest of the page blank. It's for year three to fill. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close: the porch
696.hook: the school of the porch is yours to visit any time
696.howItsDone: Some people who study the Stoics keep returning to a handful of texts, the Handbook, Seneca's letters and the Meditations, rereading them over the years as guides rather than rulebooks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahead, to the big questions. Your line was the big questions. Did you write yours at the top of a blank page? Leave it there. Day six hundred ninety-six. The last day of year two.

A porch is a strange kind of room. It has a roof, so you can shelter there. It has no front wall, so the street comes right up to it. People stop on the steps to talk, to wait out the rain, to watch the evening come in. Nobody checks a ticket. You can stay an hour or a minute, and come back whenever you like. A school of philosophy started on exactly that kind of porch. We have spent a whole year sitting on it. Today we close year two.
screen: `A ROOF, BUT NO FRONT WALL.` → `NOBODY CHECKS A TICKET.` → `A YEAR ON THE PORCH.`

segments.voice: First, what a porch asks of you. On day six hundred eighty-nine we stood in Athens at the painted porch where Zeno taught in the open. Notice what that means. Nobody enrolls on a porch. You step up from the street, and you can step down again. Second, how the Handbook sends you off. Near its end, in a passage we met on day three hundred eighty-five, Epictetus turns to his student and asks: how long will you put it off? You are not a boy any more. The contest is now; it can't be postponed. Then he points to Socrates, who became who he was by attending to reason in everything, and says: you are not yet a Socrates, but you can live as someone who wants to be one. The book doesn't end with a diploma. It ends by pointing at today. Third, not finished, and that's fine. Nobody leaves a year of reading as a sage. Epictetus asked his students to show him even one Stoic and implied he'd never seen one; Seneca said plainly that he wasn't wise. What the porch offers instead is a direction: wanting to be the kind of person Socrates was, and taking the next step on an ordinary day. Fourth, the porch stays open. A porch has no door to lock behind you. Whatever you kept from this year, a morning intention, an evening question, a delayed reply, you can step back up onto it any day you want. Tomorrow, year three: six questions.
screen: `NOBODY ENROLLS ON A PORCH.` · `HOW LONG WILL YOU PUT IT OFF?` · `NOT YET A SOCRATES.` · `A PORCH HAS NO DOOR TO LOCK.` · then, large: `THE PORCH STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Find a step, if you can: a porch, a stoop, a front step, a stair in your building. Or sit in a doorway, half in and half out. Sit down. Feel the roof or the sky above you, and the open side in front. Let the year come to you as one picture: whichever teacher, line or moment stayed. Don't sort it or grade it. Just sit with it, the way people sit on steps at the end of a day. The bell holds the time.
Socrates, the model Epictetus points to at the Handbook's end: not yet him, but someone who wants to be. Today's word, and the last of year two.
Your line: the porch stays open. Choose one Stoic habit to carry into year three, and do it once more tonight. Then rest. Tomorrow, six questions. Day six hundred ninety-six.

697.title: Six questions
697.hook: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: the questions under every tradition
697.howItsDone: People who read across traditions often keep a running list of their own big questions and return to the same texts with them over the years, reading for what each text asks as well as what it answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed year two with Socrates as the model, on a porch with no door. Your line was the porch stays open. Did you carry one Stoic habit over the line into the new year? Bring it along. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

"What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" That line is a question. It sits in the eighth Psalm, in a book of prayers and songs, and the psalm asks it while looking up at the night sky. The old books do this. In the middle of the teaching, the text turns around and asks. Year three starts right there. Not with answers. With questions the texts themselves ask, the ones we'll carry to each tradition this year. There are six.
screen: `WHAT IS MAN?` → `THE PSALM JUST ASKS.` → `YEAR THREE STARTS WITH QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: First, the texts ask, too. It's easy to treat scripture and old philosophy as a place to look things up. But listen to how often they speak in questions. Second, suffering and death, and the book of Job asks both. Job, sitting in the ashes, says: "Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul?" Later in the book: "If a man die, shall he live again?" Those are the first two questions of our year. Suffering, then death. Third, love, work and forgiveness. In Kahlil Gibran's book The Prophet, a woman named Almitra stands up and says, "Speak to us of Love." She doesn't ask whether love matters. She asks to hear about it. On work, the Teacher in Ecclesiastes asks, "What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?" And on forgiveness, in Matthew's Gospel, Peter comes to Jesus with a question that has a number in it: "Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" Fourth, awe, which takes us back to the eighth Psalm: what is man, that thou art mindful of him? That's the sixth question, and the last block of our year. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Each one gets its own long stretch of days, in that order. And across those days we'll hear the Buddha and Job, the Gospels and Rumi, the Stoics, poets and scientists, each answering in its own voice. Nobody here hands you the answer key. The questions come first, because an answer only means something once you know what it's answering.
screen: `THE TEXTS ASK, TOO.` · `SUFFERING AND DEATH: JOB ASKS.` · `LOVE, WORK, FORGIVENESS.` · `AWE: WHAT IS MAN?` · then, large: `THE BIG SIX.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Take one of today's lines, whichever stayed with you: Job's if a man die, shall he live again; Peter's how oft shall I forgive; the psalm's what is man. Say it slowly, inwardly, as a question put to you rather than a quotation. When an answer jumps up, set it down, and ask the line again. Let the question stand open, the way the verse leaves it standing. The bell holds the time.
Six questions: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, asked inside the old texts themselves, and the shape of year three. Today's word.
Your line: the big six. Once today, catch one of the six turning up as a real question, in the news, at work, in a conversation, and name which of the six it is. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

what it means: six questions the old texts themselves ask, heard before anyone tries to answer them.

698.title: Answers kept apart
698.hook: this year each tradition answers in its own voice, and we don't blend them into one
698.howItsDone: Some interfaith study groups let each tradition speak in its own texts and terms, and ask members of that tradition to explain it, rather than merging teachings into one shared answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six questions, asked inside the old texts themselves. Your line was the big six. Did one of them turn up as a real question in your day? Keep it close. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

Squeeze every tube in a child's paint box onto one plate and stir. Red, blue, yellow, green, the lovely violet. What you get is brown. Every color was beautiful on its own, and together, stirred, they cancel each other out. Wisdom from many traditions can go the same way. Take a little from here and a little from there, stir it into one soft answer, and you end up with something nobody actually holds. This year we are going to hear a great many answers. So before the first one, a rule for how we hear them.
screen: `STIR EVERY COLOR TOGETHER.` → `YOU GET BROWN.` → `A RULE BEFORE THE FIRST ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, a blended answer belongs to nobody. Take the question of suffering. The Buddha names craving as where it comes from. Job, in the ashes, argues his case before God. Stir those together into everything happens for a reason, and you've lost both of them. So this year every answer is named. The Buddha's is the Buddha's. Job's is Job's. Second, each answer comes with a life. A teaching isn't a loose sentence floating in the air. It lives inside practices, a community, a long line of people who read it and argued about it. To hear it well you have to hear where it lives. Third, alike is not the same. Some lines across traditions do sound close. Before long we'll hear the Dhammapada say that hatred ceases by love, and later in the year Jesus will say, love your enemies. Those can sit side by side as neighbors. But one belongs to the Buddha's sayings in the Dhammapada, the other to the Sermon on the Mount, and each makes the most sense in its own house. So we'll notice the echo, and leave each line at home. Fourth, swift to hear. The letter of James puts it plainly: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." And from a very different house, the Stoic Zeno is reported by the old biographer Diogenes Laertius to have said that we have two ears and one mouth so that we might listen more and talk less. Two houses, two sayings, each in its own words, and neither needs the other to make its point. Together they set this year's rule: hear the answer out before you reply to it.
screen: `A BLENDED ANSWER BELONGS TO NOBODY.` · `EACH ANSWER COMES WITH A LIFE.` · `ALIKE IS NOT THE SAME.` · `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · then, large: `LISTEN FIRST.`

segments.voice: Settle, and listen to the room for a moment. Pick out one sound, then another, without naming them good or bad. Just hear them. Now make yourself a small promise, in your own words, for the year: that when a tradition answers one of the six questions, you'll hear it out to the end before you agree, disagree, or start mixing it with something else. You don't have to say it aloud. Just make it, and then go back to listening to the room. The bell holds the time.
Diogenes Laertius, the ancient biographer who credits Zeno with saying we have two ears and one mouth so we might listen more and talk less. Today's word.
Your line: listen first. In one conversation today, let the other person finish completely before you answer. Notice what you hear in the part you'd usually talk over. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

699.title: Why do we suffer?
699.hook: every tradition asks it, and each answers differently
699.howItsDone: Some people bring suffering to their own tradition's texts and teachers: Christians to the Gospels and prayer, Muslims to the Qur'an and the practice of patience, Buddhists to the four noble truths, students of Stoicism to the Handbook.

segments.voice: Yesterday: answers kept apart, as Diogenes Laertius records it, each tradition in its own house. Your line was listen first. Did someone finish a whole sentence today without you stepping on the end of it? Day six hundred ninety-nine.

A man blind from birth is sitting by the road. A teacher and his students walk past, and the students ask the question out loud, right there. Whose fault is this? Did this man do something wrong, or did his parents? It's an old question, and a hard one to hear about yourself. When something terrible happens, the nearest reason to hand is often blame. Today we open the first great question of the year: why do we suffer? We'll start by hearing four answers, each in its own voice.
screen: `A MAN BLIND FROM BIRTH.` → `WHOSE FAULT IS THIS?` → `THE FIRST GREAT QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the Gospel of John. The disciples ask, "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" And Jesus answers, "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Then he heals him. There is a lot in the rest of that answer, but its first word is plain: neither. The shortcut to blame is closed. Second, the Qur'an. In the second surah, God says that people will be tried with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops, and then: give glad tidings to the steadfast. Hardship, in this answer, is a test, and the response it asks for is steadfastness. The Arabic word behind it is sabr, patience that holds. Third, the Buddha. In his first teaching he names suffering, then names where it comes from: a craving, a thirst, that keeps reaching for more and for something else. We'll spend the coming days inside that answer. Fourth, the Stoic Epictetus. In his Handbook he says that what troubles people isn't the things that happen, but their judgments about them. Death isn't terrible, he says, or Socrates would have thought so; the terror is in our opinion of death. Four answers. A test met with patience. A thirst. A judgment. And a story where blame is refused, and the story moves on to healing. They don't line up into one tidy reply, and this year won't force them to. They sit at the same table and each speaks for itself.
screen: `WHO SINNED? NEITHER.` · `THE QUR'AN: TRIED, AND STEADFAST.` · `THE BUDDHA: A THIRST.` · `EPICTETUS: OUR JUDGMENTS.` · then, large: `EACH ANSWERS DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breathing slow down on its own. Now, gently, name one suffering you carry. Not the worst thing that ever happened, unless that's what comes. Just one real weight: an ache, a worry, a loss, a strain at home. Don't put it into words yet; just let it be in the room with you. Then, without picking a side, let the four answers pass by it, like four visitors at a bedside. A test. A thirst. A judgment. Neither he nor his parents. You don't have to agree with any of them. Just notice which visitor you'd let stay a little longer. The bell holds the time.
Sabr, the Arabic word for patience that holds steady under trial, the response the Qur'an asks of the steadfast. Today's word.
Your line: each answers differently. When you hear someone explain why something bad happened today, on the news or at work, listen for which answer they reached for. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

700.title: Name it first
700.hook: the Buddha names suffering first, the way a doctor names an illness (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
700.carry: stand next to it and look
700.howItsDone: Buddhists learn the four noble truths as the heart of the Buddha's first teaching, and some meditation teachers begin by asking students to notice and name their experience plainly before trying to change it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: why do we suffer? Four answers, sabr among them, and your line was each answers differently. Did you hear someone reach for one of them today? Now we step inside the Buddha's answer. Day seven hundred.

"It's making a noise." "What kind of noise?" "A bad one." "When does it happen?" "I don't know, sometimes." A mechanic can't do a thing with that until it gets more precise. A grinding when you brake. A click when you turn left. Once the noise has a plain name, the work can start. It's easy to treat our own troubles the other way round. We fix, we distract, we explain, and we never quite say what the noise is. The Buddha's first teaching starts somewhere else. It starts by naming.
screen: `WHAT KIND OF NOISE?` → `NAMED PLAINLY, THEN FIXED.` → `THE BUDDHA STARTS BY NAMING.`

segments.voice: First, a plain list. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha's first teaching lays out four noble truths, and the first is suffering, dukkha. He doesn't describe it with drama. He lists it: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering. Then three more: being joined with what you dislike, being parted from what you love, not getting what you want. Second, look at that last one. Not getting what you want. It sits on the same list as death. The text puts them on one list, without ranking them. A canceled plan and a funeral can both find a place there. Third, the first task is to understand it. In the same teaching, each truth comes with its own job. Suffering is to be fully understood. Its origin is to be let go. Its ending is to be realized. The path is to be developed. So the very first job the Buddha gives suffering isn't fix it, or escape it, or explain it away. It's understand it, all the way through. Teachers sometimes use a picture for this: a good doctor names the illness before writing the prescription. Fourth, named before it's fixed. A name is a small thing, but it changes where you stand. When the trouble is a fog, you're inside it. When it has a plain name, aging, illness, being parted from someone, not getting what I wanted, you can stand next to it and look. The cause, the ending and the path all come later. In the Buddha's order, naming comes first.

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Find one pain you're carrying right now. It can be in the body, or in a relationship, or a small frustration from this morning. Now name it plainly, the way the old list does. Just a few words: this is worry about money. This is missing my brother. This is a sore back. No because, no should, no story. If the story starts, come back to the plain name and say it again, quietly. Then sit beside it for the rest of the time, the way you'd sit beside a friend on a bench, close but not inside their trouble. The bell holds the time.
Dukkha, the Buddha's word for suffering, from birth and aging to not getting what you want, named plainly so it can be understood. Today's word.
Your line: stand next to it and look. The next time something goes wrong today, before you fix it or vent about it, give it its plain name, once, in your head. Day seven hundred.
